title: WorldFailBench: Do World Models Understand Policy Failures?

paper.title: WorldFailBench: Do World Models Understand Policy Failures?
paper.abstract: Abstract Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generalist robot policies increasingly support diverse manipulation tasks [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , with advances in multimodal prompting, bimanual control, and hierarchical reasoning [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Reliable deployment requires repeated evaluation across tasks and operating conditions. Physical testing occupies robot hardware and requires resets and supervision [ 8 , 9 ] , while traditional simulation requires scene construction and adaptation to the target environment [ 10 ] . Learned world models offer a complementary route: predicting future observations conditioned on robot actions [ 11 , 12 ] enables closed-loop policy evaluation before physical deployment [ 13 , 14 ] . To serve as reliable policy evaluators, they should faithfully simulate policy behavior in the target environments. Recent benchmarks, including WorldArena and WMBench, systematically assess the reliability of world models as policy evaluators in simulated and real-world settings [ 15 , 16 ] . A common approach is outcome-based evaluation [ 17 , 13 , 14 , 18 ] . Specifically, the same policies are evaluated in a world model and a reference environment , either a conventional simulator or a real-world robot setup. Policy success rates in the two environments are compared through cross-policy correlations. Reported agreement with real-world policy performance provides encouraging evidence for the use of world models as policy evaluators [ 19 , 20 ] . However, outcome-based evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how a policy fails. Figure 1 illustrates three discrepancies in cloth collection and their implications for policy assessment. (1) Failure reason. In panel A, reference execution attempts to grasp the cloth but drops it, indicating an action execution failure. The generated rollout instead attempts to grasp the basket, choosing the wrong target and indicating a task planning failure . Although both executions fail, this mismatch can misattribute an execution problem to task planning and direct policy improvement toward the wrong component. (2) Failure stage. In panel B, reference execution fails during placement, whereas the model predicts failure during transport. This misrepresents where execution breaks down despite agreement on the final outcome. (3) Failure boundary. Panel C illustrates how a model can continue to predict high success rates after basket displacement causes reference success to collapse. Missing this success-to-failure transition can overestimate the conditions under which a policy operates reliably. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure during closed-loop interaction? Figure 1 : Failure discrepancies in cloth collection. (A) Failure reason: dropping the cloth versus grasping the basket. (B) Failure stage: reference placement versus model transport. (C) Failure boundary: missed transitions under basket displacement. To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three complementary evaluation tasks. Failure reason asks whether a world model reproduces the kinds of observable errors a policy makes in the reference environment. We compare each policy’s type-specific failure frequencies over all evaluation episodes and the correlation of these frequencies across policies in the two environments. Failure stage asks whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution as in the reference environment. We compare each policy’s stage-specific failure frequencies over the same episodes and their cross-policy correlation between the two environments. Failure boundary asks whether the model captures the conditions under which a policy transitions from success to failure. In simulation, we select pairs of nearby conditions with a drop in reference success rate and test whether the model reproduces the direction and magnitude of that drop. The benchmark spans manipulation tasks in the LIBERO [ 21 ] and RoboTwin [ 22 ] simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Table 1 compares benchmark designs. Experiments with seven world models reveal diagnostic gaps that outcome-based evaluation does not expose. On RoboTwin, average errors in predicted planning and execution failure frequencies range from 15.9 to 33.5 percentage points. All seven models show weak stage-specific policy correlations, including the model that best tracks policy success rates. Under scene changes, the models also fail to reliably capture success-to-failure transitions: 95.2% of their responses on the tested RoboTwin boundary pairs understate the magnitude of reference success-rate changes. Our contributions are: • We introduce WorldFailBench, which evaluates world-model fidelity from three complementary perspectives: failure types, failure stages, and failure boundaries. • We collect reference and model rollouts with failure annotations in LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation and on the G1 robot, and construct controlled boundary pairs in simulation. • Extensive experiments with seven world models show that outcome-based agreement does not ensure faithful failure diagnosis or boundary prediction, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation. sections.heading: World-model-based policy evaluation and benchmarks.
sections.text: Learned world models increasingly serve as interactive surrogate environments for evaluating embodied policies. A recent survey distinguishes evaluation targets, protocols, metrics, and data when interpreting world-model benchmark results [ 32 ] . Systems such as WorldEval, WorldGym, and dWorldEval use action-conditioned video generation to estimate policy performance and compare policy rankings [ 17 , 13 , 18 ] , while GigaWorld-1 investigates how world-model architectures affect long-horizon, action-faithful evaluation [ 16 ] . WorldArena provides unified benchmark protocols for embodied world models; WorldArena 2.0 extends evaluation to visuotactile inputs, policy optimization, and cross-embodiment sim-to-real settings [ 15 , 23 ] . Beyond policy-outcome evaluation, related benchmarks assess complementary aspects of world-model fidelity: WorldSimBench and EWMBench probe perceptual, motion, and semantic consistency [ 25 , 24 ] ; RoboWM-Bench tests whether generated interactions translate into executable behaviors [ 26 ] ; MiraBench analyzes reliability and over-optimism under failure-inducing actions [ 31 ] ; and RoboEval provides structured, stage-aware policy assessments [ 30 ] . Table 1 summarizes these evaluation designs. Existing benchmarks provide outcome, executability, or recovery signals, but do not jointly assess agreement with reference execution in observable failure types, decisive failure stages, and local success-to-failure boundaries. WorldFailBench evaluates these three aspects through paired reference and model rollouts and controlled boundary interventions.

sections.heading: Fine-grained robotic failure analysis.
sections.text: Diagnosing failure modes is essential for reliable policy deployment and interpretable robot learning. Prior methods explain manipulation failures through multimodal reasoning [ 33 , 34 ] , monitor runtime consistency and execution progress [ 35 ] , or provide structured, stage-aware policy assessment [ 30 ] . RoboReward and FailBench evaluate automated success detectors and reward models [ 36 , 37 ] . These approaches assess policies or automated judges against reference executions. WorldFailBench uses paired reference and model rollouts to evaluate how faithfully generative world models reproduce observable failure types, stage distributions, and local success-to-failure boundaries.

sections.heading: 3 WorldFailBench
sections.text: WorldFailBench evaluates whether world models preserve policy failure behavior. Figure 2 summarizes the comparison: corresponding closed-loop executions provide failure-type and stage annotations, while controlled scene variations reveal success-to-failure conditions. We next describe the execution protocol, metrics, and benchmark construction. Figure 2 : Overview of WorldFailBench: comparing reference and world-model rollouts through failure reason, failure stage, and failure boundary.

sections.heading: 3.1 Closed-Loop Evaluation Framework
sections.text: Closed-loop evaluation tests whether a policy exhibits consistent failure behavior when acting on generated rather than reference observations. At each step, the policy selects an action from its observation history, robot state, and task instruction; the world model predicts the next observation and returns it to the policy. Reference execution follows the same feedback process through a simulator or physical robot (Figure 2 ). Each loop selects its own subsequent actions, allowing model-generated feedback to affect policy behavior. To establish a common basis for comparing policy failures, we fix the task instruction, policy, and corresponding initial conditions across environments. Appendix A.3 provides further details of the rollout setup.

sections.text: Failure Reason and Failure Stage compare failure frequencies and cross-policy correlations; Failure Boundary tests conditions under which policies transition from success to failure. sections.heading: Failure-reason and failure-stage records.
sections.text: For each task–policy setting, we collect 50 reference rollouts from randomized scenes and corresponding world-model executions using Section 3.1 . Both successful and failed rollouts enter annotation and frequency evaluation. Figure 3 (a,b) shows reference failure counts by type and episode counts by the number of task stages, respectively.

sections.heading: Boundary pairs.
sections.text: On RoboTwin and LIBERO, we scan one scene factor—object position, orientation, or size—while holding other conditions fixed. Ten reference executions per condition identify adjacent pairs with a success-rate difference of at least δ = 0.3 \delta=0.3 (30 percentage points). We freeze 60 pairs per platform and their endpoint order, then independently re-estimate reference success using fresh random seeds (Appendix C ). For illustration, a LIBERO position scan in 2 cm increments might show reference success falling from 90% at a 4 cm offset to 40% at 6 cm, qualifying the pair for selection. These hypothetical rates illustrate the criterion, rather than an additional measured pair. Each world model runs the same policy ten times per frozen endpoint. Pairs are not reselected or reordered after re-estimation. Figure 3 (c) gives pair counts by factor.

sections.heading: Annotation and quality control.
sections.text: We use two annotation stages. (1) Outcome annotation. Doubao-Seed-2-1-Pro and ChatGPT 6 annotate video outcomes for reference and model rollouts, achieving 90.1% agreement. One expert adjudicates all disagreements. We randomly audit agreed samples totaling 10% of the full dataset, obtaining 97% agreement with human judgments. For simulated reference executions, final outcomes follow native simulator predicates; video labels serve as verification. World-model rollouts and real-world G1 executions use adjudicated video labels. (2) Failure annotation. Two experts label the failure type and stage of every confirmed failure, achieving 92% inter-annotator agreement before adjudication. A third annotator resolves all disagreements. Appendix B details annotation rules and outcome verification.

sections.heading: 4.2 Failure-Type Understanding
sections.text: RQ1: Does agreement in policy success rates extend to failure-type fidelity? An evaluator must reproduce the kinds of failures behind the outcomes to support diagnosis of policy weaknesses. We compare success-rate and failure-type correlations across the same five RoboTwin policies (Figure 4 ), then measure errors in individual policies’ failure frequencies using TFE (Table 3 ). Figure 4 : RoboTwin mean within-task Pearson correlations for (a) success rate, (b) Task Planning, and (c) Action Execution. Ref–Ref is the reference-repeatability baseline; each correlation uses five policies. (1) Success-rate correlation does not establish consistent agreement across failure types. DW05 has the highest success-rate correlation (0.597), but lower correlations for planning (0.456) and execution failures (0.348). Agreement also differs in direction across types: A2World correlates positively with reference planning failures (0.353) but negatively with execution failures ( − 0.086 -0.086 ), while BWM shows the opposite pattern ( − 0.121 -0.121 versus 0.143). The highest aggregate TPC is 0.402 (Table 15 ). Thus, an evaluator’s ability to compare policies depends on which failure type is being assessed; its overall success-rate correlation does not describe this distinction. (2) World models misestimate how often policies exhibit planning and execution failures, distorting the diagnosis of their weaknesses. Across the seven models, the average absolute error in these failure frequencies is 15.9–33.5 percentage points (Table 3 ). Generated rollouts therefore give an inaccurate picture of how commonly each kind of failure occurs. For policy evaluation, these frequencies describe the prevalence of specific weaknesses, whereas the overall success rate records only how often tasks are completed. Across all seven models, SPC ranges from − 0.123 -0.123 to 0.095. Ref–Ref attains 0.942 for success rate and 0.903 for stages, showing that both comparisons are substantially more reproducible between reference runs. The models’ relative strength in outcome evaluation therefore does not carry over to comparing where policies fail during full-task execution. (2) Generated rollouts misrepresent stage frequencies and can relocate the dominant failure. Mean SFE ranges from 0.633 to 0.817. The FastWAM case in Figure 5 shows what this distortion means: in blocks_ranking_size , reference failures concentrate at Grasp small (66%), with 16% at Place, whereas DreamDojo reports 6% and 46%, respectively. This shift from grasping to placement appears across all five policies (Figure 10 ). The resulting diagnosis attributes the main breakdown in full-task execution to a different stage, information that an overall success rate does not provide.

sections.text: RQ3: Do world models reproduce policy failure boundaries under scene changes? We test whether generated rollouts identify which conditions reduce policy reliability and by how much. Thus, selecting the best model for each factor still leaves substantial disagreement about which nearby condition is less reliable. By comparison, Ref–Ref yields OA of 0.95–1.00 and GE of 0.005–0.020 across the three factors. Predicted changes also tend to be too small: across seven models on the same 60 RoboTwin boundary pairs, 400 of 420 model–pair comparisons (95.2%) underestimate the absolute reference success-rate difference (Figure 11 a–c). Four models predict an increase, and one predicts no change. Only A2World and GE-Sim identify the decline, but both predict a decrease of just 20 percentage points. Even a correct direction therefore leaves most of the reliability loss unrepresented in this case. For a policy evaluator, these errors can lead to overly optimistic robustness assessments by obscuring both the conditions that trigger failure and the severity of the resulting reliability loss. (2) Different scene changes expose distinct weaknesses in world-model policy evaluation. Five of the seven models have their lowest OA on orientation changes, while DW05 and GE-Sim have their lowest OA on size changes (Table 6 ). Ctrl-World illustrates this dependence: its OA falls from 75.8% for size to 35.9% for orientation, where it also has the highest GE among the seven models (0.719). GE-Sim exhibits the opposite pattern, with OA reaching 59.0% for orientation but only 42.4% for size. Testing size alone would miss Ctrl-World’s difficulty with rotation, whereas testing orientation alone would miss GE-Sim’s weaker size predictions. An evaluator that captures a policy’s sensitivity to one scene factor may therefore misjudge its vulnerability to another. Failure-boundary evaluation makes this limitation explicit: it assesses whether a world model can support judgments about policy robustness under specific scene changes and identifies where its predictions require reference-environment verification before guiding further testing.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced WorldFailBench to evaluate whether world models preserve policy failure behavior beyond success rates. By comparing generated rollouts with reference executions, it measures agreement in failure types, failure stages, and responses to scene changes near failure boundaries. Across the evaluated models, agreement in policy success rates did not consistently extend to failure diagnosis. Models with stronger outcome correlations could still misrepresent which failures occurred or when they occurred, while generated rollouts often understated the effects of scene changes on success. These findings show why failure fidelity matters when using world models to interpret policy behavior. Our evaluation covers a finite set of policies, tasks, and boundary conditions, which limits the generality of these findings. The results characterize complete world-model systems, including their adapters and rollout schedules, and do not isolate individual architectural components. Failure labels describe observable behavior without establishing internal policy causes. Future work will extend the evaluation to broader settings and examine whether assessing failure fidelity improves policy training.

sections.heading: Sweeping trash.
sections.text: Success requires the main target trash to be swept into the dustpan using the broom. Tiny, visually ambiguous fragments may be tolerated; clearly visible larger pieces remaining outside preclude success.

sections.heading: Collecting clothes.
sections.text: Success requires the target clothing to be placed in the basket and released. Partial draping over the rim is acceptable when the basket supports the clothing; suspension above the basket or continued support by the hand does not satisfy the goal.

sections.heading: A.2 Environment, Model, and Policy Configurations
sections.text: Evaluation scope. WorldFailBench evaluates complete world-model systems, including their platform adapters, state-feedback rules, and execution schedules. These components vary across models and jointly determine their capabilities for closed-loop policy evaluation. We therefore follow each model’s official implementation and inference procedure, adapting observation and action interfaces to the target platform where necessary.

sections.heading: A.3.1 Reference scenes and initial conditions
sections.text: RoboTwin. We use demo_clean with seen instructions. This setting retains task-specific randomization of object positions, orientations, and assets while disabling background, clutter, lighting, camera-position, and table-height perturbations. Candidate scene seeds start at 200000 and increase sequentially. Candidate scenes are checked using expert planning and task-success tests; accepted scenes are then reinitialized before executing the evaluated policy. We collect 50 accepted scenes for each task–policy pair. The accepted seed sequences differ across RoboTwin policies. Episode indices are local to each task–policy collection. Within such a collection, all world models share the corresponding retained reference episodes. Cross-policy frequency comparisons aggregate each policy’s task-level scene sample; they do not rely on episode-wise matching between policies. LIBERO. For each task, we restore official initial-state indices 0–49 using collector seed 7 and perform ten settling steps before policy execution. These settling steps are excluded from the policy-action budget. We do not add pose or appearance perturbations to this initial-state set in the failure-type and failure-stage evaluations. Cross-policy scene pairing is established using the task definition, initial-state-file hash, and initial-state index. G1. Each generated rollout is associated with a real execution through its task, policy version, and source UID. Initialization uses that execution’s recorded initial RGB observation and 26D robot state. The source UID defines reference–model pairing. Different policy versions follow shared reset procedures but retain their own real-execution records.

sections.heading: A.3.2 Reference–model pairing and random seeds
sections.text: Reference–model pairing fixes the task, policy checkpoint, source episode identity, initial RGB observation, initial robot state, and instruction. Within each task–policy setting, all models are scored on the same retained episode set. Scene seeds identify candidate environments, policy seeds govern policy sampling, and generation seeds govern world-model sampling. The retained RoboTwin collection launchers specify default policy seeds of 0 for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 42 for LingBot-VLA-v2 and FastWAM. Generation follows each implementation’s seed schedule; BWM, for example, uses 42 + k for generation block k. The 50 reference episodes sample different accepted scenes or initial-state indices. These are scene-level samples rather than repeated trials of one fixed scene.

sections.heading: A.3.3 Initialization, action consumption, and state feedback
sections.text: Initialization. Each world-model execution receives its source reference episode’s initial RGB observation, robot state, and instruction. On RoboTwin, the BWM and DW05 implementations also use the first recorded reference action chunk for initialization. Reference-action conditioning is confined to initialization. Subsequent reference images, robot states, and actions do not condition generated execution; reference videos remain available for scoring. Closed-loop execution. At each interaction round, the policy predicts an action sequence from the current observation and robot state, conditioned on the task instruction. Each world model advances the rollout according to its supported temporal configuration, then returns the corresponding observation and state for the next policy call. The final frame retained for the consumed action interval becomes the next observation, paired with the robot state at the same point on the action timeline. Robot-state feedback. GE-Sim jointly predicts images and states; its predicted state corresponding to the retained image is fed to the policy. The other models propagate robot state from the consumed policy actions using their platform-specific update routines, including the corresponding coordinate and gripper conventions. These updates start from the recorded initial state and do not read subsequent reference states. Reference execution advances through the simulator or physical robot using the same fixed policy checkpoint. After initialization, reference and generated executions obtain actions from their respective feedback streams. Their later action sequences may therefore differ even when their source initial conditions are matched.

sections.heading: A.3.4 Rollout budget
sections.text: Following WorldArena [ 15 ] , we set the world-model execution budget to 1.2 times the corresponding reference duration on all three platforms. This duration is converted to each model’s action and frame timeline, with rounding to its supported temporal windows. To assess possible premature truncation on RoboTwin, we sample five failed episodes that reached the original rollout limit for each task–policy–world-model configuration (20 tasks, five policies, and seven world models), yielding 3,500 episodes. We extend the rollout horizon to the task-specific maximum episode length specified by the simulator. Only 17 episodes (0.49%) succeed under the extended budget, indicating that failure outcomes in the sampled episodes are largely stable under longer evaluation horizons.

sections.heading: A.4 Reference Repeatability (Ref–Ref)
sections.text: To assess the reproducibility of failure measurements, we independently rerun the policies in RoboTwin and LIBERO under the same evaluation settings. For failure-reason and failure-stage evaluation, we collect 50 new rollouts per task–policy setting from the same initial scenes, matching the original reference collection. We compare the two reference collections using the same annotation procedure, metrics, and aggregation rules. The resulting Ref–Ref scores provide an empirical baseline for interpreting reference–model discrepancies relative to the variation observed between independent reference executions. For failure-boundary evaluation, Ref–Ref compares success-rate changes between two reference estimates at paired scene conditions using OA and GE (Section 3.2.3 ). The two estimates are obtained from independent batches of reference executions collected after the boundary pairs and their endpoint order have been fixed. Neither estimate uses the discovery rollouts, and the pairs and endpoint order remain unchanged for this comparison. Tables 6 and 19 report reference repeatability separately for position, orientation, and size changes.

sections.heading: Appendix B Annotation Protocol
sections.text: This appendix defines failure labels and annotation decisions, followed by the outcome annotation prompt.

sections.heading: B.1 Failure Categories and Annotation Rules
sections.text: The two interpretable failure types adapt the planning/execution distinction in REFLECT [ 33 ] and Guardian [ 38 ] to trajectory annotation. Labels describe observable behavior in the context of the task instruction, without establishing internal policy causes. The examples below illustrate the definitions and are not additional measured trials.

sections.heading: Task Planning Failure.
sections.text: This category concerns task-inappropriate choices of targets, subgoals, or their ordering. It includes omitting a required step or attempting a subgoal before its prerequisites are satisfied. For example, closing a cabinet before inserting the required object, then attempting insertion through the closed door, violates a task dependency even if the closing motion succeeds.

sections.heading: Action Execution Failure.
sections.text: This category concerns failure to carry out an intended subgoal through motion or physical interaction. Examples include missing a grasp, dropping a held object during transport, and inaccurate placement. For example, the gripper approaches the intended mug but closes beside its handle and lifts without the mug. The observed interaction fails to achieve the intended grasp.

sections.heading: Indeterminate Failure.
sections.text: A confirmed failure is indeterminate when its primary type cannot be identified reliably, for example because the decisive interaction is occluded. This label is recorded as Unjudgable . These episodes remain in the all-episode denominator. TFE and TPC evaluate Task Planning and Action Execution. Figure 8 illustrates observable task-planning and action-execution failures with task instructions and frame sequences. Figure 8 : Examples of task-planning and action-execution failures. (a) The robot arranges blocks in a row instead of the instructed tower, or attempts to place soap without first opening the drawer. (b) A released bottle tips and rolls away, or placing the third bowl disrupts the stack. Frames proceed from left to right; red boxes mark the relevant objects and interactions. These cases illustrate the two interpretable failure categories.

sections.heading: Outcome assessment and verification.
sections.text: Final outcome labels for reference executions in RoboTwin and LIBERO follow the simulator’s native task predicates. World-model rollouts and real-world G1 executions are assessed from video by two VLMs, with one expert adjudicating disagreements. To verify consistency between video-based and simulator-based outcome assessment, we compare video annotations with native task predicates on a random 10% sample of reference simulation videos, obtaining 99.8% agreement.

sections.heading: Type and stage assignment.
sections.text: For each confirmed failure, two experts label one primary type and one decisive stage; a third expert adjudicates disagreements. When several errors occur, the type follows the earliest clearly supported primary cause; the stage identifies the earliest decisive event preventing completion. Stage names are copied from the task-specific list. Timestamps and critical-moment descriptions identify repeated occurrences; stage categories follow the task-specific decomposition in Appendix A.1 . If a stage cannot be identified, annotators record it as unknown . Reference and model executions use the same rules; successful episodes contribute zero failure counts.

sections.heading: B.3 Outcome Annotation Prompt
sections.text: The following prompt specifies video-based outcome evaluation. The placeholders {task} and {instruction} supply the task name and language instruction. The prompt requests a JSON response. ROLE AND OBJECTIVE You are a robotic task video evaluator. Determine whether the task was successfully completed based on the task instruction and the visible outcomes in the video. INPUTS Task name: {task} Task instruction: {instruction} EVALUATION RULES 1. Determine success by whether a visually identifiable task-completion state is achieved during the execution. The initial state alone does not establish success for a new execution. Once completion is observed, set success=true , even if the state changes afterward or the video continues. Do not assess whether the execution procedure was proper. 2. A blurry but reasonably identifiable completion state is sufficient for success=true . If no completion state is observed and the visible evidence supports that the task remains incomplete at the end of the video, set success=false . 3. For generated videos, ignore visual artifacts when they do not prevent outcome assessment. Focus on whether the task goal was achieved. Lower confidence when uncertain. 4. Rely only on the task instruction and visible evidence in the video. Do not infer the outcome from success/failure folder names or model names. 5. If the available visual evidence is insufficient to determine whether the task was completed, set success="unjudgeable" . Blur, a limited camera view, or an object being out of view does not by itself imply failure; use "unjudgeable" when these limitations prevent a reliable outcome judgment. 6. success_timestamp_sec is the approximate time in seconds when the task completion state first appears. Set it to null when success=false or success=unjudgeable . 7. Include only visually observable evidence in evidence. Do not classify the failure type or failure stage in this evaluation. In the JSON response, success must be true, false, or the string "unjudgeable". OUTPUT FORMAT Return only valid JSON, without Markdown: { "success": true, "success_timestamp_sec": 0.0, "reason": "<rationale and uncertainty>", "evidence": [ "<visible evidence>" ], "confidence": 0.0 }

sections.heading: C.2 Boundary Discovery and Independent Evaluation
sections.text: Both platforms separate boundary discovery from final reference estimation using the following procedure.

sections.heading: (1) Discover candidate boundaries.
sections.text: We estimate success at adjacent conditions on each preset path using ten complete reference rollouts per endpoint. A pair qualifies when the success rates differ by at least 30 percentage points, equivalent to a difference of three successes out of ten. Both increases and decreases along the scan direction qualify. Physical pairs are deduplicated, and 20 pairs are selected for each intervention factor in each platform.

sections.heading: (2) Freeze the evaluation set.
sections.text: Before independent reference re-estimation, we fix all 60 pairs per platform, including their tasks, policies, base scenes, and endpoint conditions. Endpoints are ordered from higher to lower success according to the discovery estimates. The set and endpoint order remain fixed throughout evaluation: no pair is removed or reordered based on the re-estimated success rates, even if its difference falls below 30 percentage points or reverses direction.

sections.heading: (3) Independently re-estimate reference success.
sections.text: At every frozen endpoint in both platforms, we collect ten new reference executions using random seeds disjoint from those used for discovery. Success follows the simulator’s task predicate. All complete evaluation executions enter the estimate; exploratory probes, invalid scenes, and infrastructure errors are not counted as task failures. Only these ten new executions determine the reference success rate used for final evaluation; discovery executions are not pooled into this estimate.

sections.heading: (4) Evaluate world models.
sections.text: Each world model runs the same policy ten times at each frozen endpoint, from the corresponding initialization. OA and GE (Section 3.2.3 ) compare model success-rate changes with the independently re-estimated reference changes, using the frozen endpoint order. The reported fraction of underestimated reference changes also uses these independent estimates.

Zheng Zhang Xiaoyang Tang Shuaiqi Cheng Jiakai Huang Zhongbo Wu Ziyi Zhang Yuan Si Zeyu Liu Weibo Gao Shunyu Liu Shan You Fei Wang Xiaogang Wang Dacheng Tao Abstract Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation. 1 Introduction Generalist robot policies increasingly support diverse manipulation tasks [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , with advances in multimodal prompting, bimanual control, and hierarchical reasoning [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Reliable deployment requires repeated evaluation across tasks and operating conditions. Physical testing occupies robot hardware and requires resets and supervision [ 8 , 9 ] , while traditional simulation requires scene construction and adaptation to the target environment [ 10 ] . Learned world models offer a complementary route: predicting future observations conditioned on robot actions [ 11 , 12 ] enables closed-loop policy evaluation before physical deployment [ 13 , 14 ] . To serve as reliable policy evaluators, they should faithfully simulate policy behavior in the target environments. Recent benchmarks, including WorldArena and WMBench, systematically assess the reliability of world models as policy evaluators in simulated and real-world settings [ 15 , 16 ] . A common approach is outcome-based evaluation [ 17 , 13 , 14 , 18 ] . Specifically, the same policies are evaluated in a world model and a reference environment , either a conventional simulator or a real-world robot setup. Policy success rates in the two environments are compared through cross-policy correlations. Reported agreement with real-world policy performance provides encouraging evidence for the use of world models as policy evaluators [ 19 , 20 ] . However, outcome-based evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how a policy fails. Figure 1 illustrates three discrepancies in cloth collection and their implications for policy assessment. (1) Failure reason. In panel A, reference execution attempts to grasp the cloth but drops it, indicating an action execution failure. The generated rollout instead attempts to grasp the basket, choosing the wrong target and indicating a task planning failure . Although both executions fail, this mismatch can misattribute an execution problem to task planning and direct policy improvement toward the wrong component. (2) Failure stage. In panel B, reference execution fails during placement, whereas the model predicts failure during transport. This misrepresents where execution breaks down despite agreement on the final outcome. (3) Failure boundary. Panel C illustrates how a model can continue to predict high success rates after basket displacement causes reference success to collapse. Missing this success-to-failure transition can overestimate the conditions under which a policy operates reliably. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure during closed-loop interaction? Figure 1 : Failure discrepancies in cloth collection. (A) Failure reason: dropping the cloth versus grasping the basket. (B) Failure stage: reference placement versus model transport. (C) Failure boundary: missed transitions under basket displacement. To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three complementary evaluation tasks. Failure reason asks whether a world model reproduces the kinds of observable errors a policy makes in the reference environment. We compare each policy’s type-specific failure frequencies over all evaluation episodes and the correlation of these frequencies across policies in the two environments. Failure stage asks whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution as in the reference environment. We compare each policy’s stage-specific failure frequencies over the same episodes and their cross-policy correlation between the two environments. Failure boundary asks whether the model captures the conditions under which a policy transitions from success to failure. In simulation, we select pairs of nearby conditions with a drop in reference success rate and test whether the model reproduces the direction and magnitude of that drop. The benchmark spans manipulation tasks in the LIBERO [ 21 ] and RoboTwin [ 22 ] simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Table 1 compares benchmark designs. Experiments with seven world models reveal diagnostic gaps that outcome-based evaluation does not expose. On RoboTwin, average errors in predicted planning and execution failure frequencies range from 15.9 to 33.5 percentage points. All seven models show weak stage-specific policy correlations, including the model that best tracks policy success rates. Under scene changes, the models also fail to reliably capture success-to-failure transitions: 95.2% of their responses on the tested RoboTwin boundary pairs understate the magnitude of reference success-rate changes. Our contributions are: • We introduce WorldFailBench, which evaluates world-model fidelity from three complementary perspectives: failure types, failure stages, and failure boundaries. • We collect reference and model rollouts with failure annotations in LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation and on the G1 robot, and construct controlled boundary pairs in simulation. • Extensive experiments with seven world models show that outcome-based agreement does not ensure faithful failure diagnosis or boundary prediction, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation. Learned world models increasingly serve as interactive surrogate environments for evaluating embodied policies. A recent survey distinguishes evaluation targets, protocols, metrics, and data when interpreting world-model benchmark results [ 32 ] . Systems such as WorldEval, WorldGym, and dWorldEval use action-conditioned video generation to estimate policy performance and compare policy rankings [ 17 , 13 , 18 ] , while GigaWorld-1 investigates how world-model architectures affect long-horizon, action-faithful evaluation [ 16 ] . WorldArena provides unified benchmark protocols for embodied world models; WorldArena 2.0 extends evaluation to visuotactile inputs, policy optimization, and cross-embodiment sim-to-real settings [ 15 , 23 ] . Beyond policy-outcome evaluation, related benchmarks assess complementary aspects of world-model fidelity: WorldSimBench and EWMBench probe perceptual, motion, and semantic consistency [ 25 , 24 ] ; RoboWM-Bench tests whether generated interactions translate into executable behaviors [ 26 ] ; MiraBench analyzes reliability and over-optimism under failure-inducing actions [ 31 ] ; and RoboEval provides structured, stage-aware policy assessments [ 30 ] . Table 1 summarizes these evaluation designs. Existing benchmarks provide outcome, executability, or recovery signals, but do not jointly assess agreement with reference execution in observable failure types, decisive failure stages, and local success-to-failure boundaries. WorldFailBench evaluates these three aspects through paired reference and model rollouts and controlled boundary interventions. Fine-grained robotic failure analysis. Diagnosing failure modes is essential for reliable policy deployment and interpretable robot learning. Prior methods explain manipulation failures through multimodal reasoning [ 33 , 34 ] , monitor runtime consistency and execution progress [ 35 ] , or provide structured, stage-aware policy assessment [ 30 ] . RoboReward and FailBench evaluate automated success detectors and reward models [ 36 , 37 ] . These approaches assess policies or automated judges against reference executions. WorldFailBench uses paired reference and model rollouts to evaluate how faithfully generative world models reproduce observable failure types, stage distributions, and local success-to-failure boundaries. 3 WorldFailBench WorldFailBench evaluates whether world models preserve policy failure behavior. Figure 2 summarizes the comparison: corresponding closed-loop executions provide failure-type and stage annotations, while controlled scene variations reveal success-to-failure conditions. We next describe the execution protocol, metrics, and benchmark construction. Figure 2 : Overview of WorldFailBench: comparing reference and world-model rollouts through failure reason, failure stage, and failure boundary. 3.1 Closed-Loop Evaluation Framework Closed-loop evaluation tests whether a policy exhibits consistent failure behavior when acting on generated rather than reference observations. At each step, the policy selects an action from its observation history, robot state, and task instruction; the world model predicts the next observation and returns it to the policy. Reference execution follows the same feedback process through a simulator or physical robot (Figure 2 ). Each loop selects its own subsequent actions, allowing model-generated feedback to affect policy behavior. To establish a common basis for comparing policy failures, we fix the task instruction, policy, and corresponding initial conditions across environments. Appendix A.3 provides further details of the rollout setup. 3.2 Evaluation Tasks and Metrics Failure Reason and Failure Stage compare failure frequencies and cross-policy correlations; Failure Boundary tests conditions under which policies transition from success to failure. By comparing generated rollouts with reference executions, it measures agreement in failure types, failure stages, and responses to scene changes near failure boundaries. Across the evaluated models, agreement in policy success rates did not consistently extend to failure diagnosis. Models with stronger outcome correlations could still misrepresent which failures occurred or when they occurred, while generated rollouts often understated the effects of scene changes on success. These findings show why failure fidelity matters when using world models to interpret policy behavior. Our evaluation covers a finite set of policies, tasks, and boundary conditions, which limits the generality of these findings. The results characterize complete world-model systems, including their adapters and rollout schedules, and do not isolate individual architectural components. Failure labels describe observable behavior without establishing internal policy causes. Future work will extend the evaluation to broader settings and examine whether assessing failure fidelity improves policy training.
